Hadama's three circles theorem, which expresses the area of a region in terms of its boundary length, has been expanded to apply to functions with multiple variables. This research proves a higher-dimensional equivalent of the theorem for functions that have a specific property and are defined on a specific type of area. In doing so, it identifies the length of the boundary that appears in Hadama's formula and provides a connection to a broader class of functions known as monogenic functions. This new understanding can be applied to simplify and solve certain complex boundary value problems. Additionally, this research results in a new generalization of the area formula for circles in three-dimensional space.

The process of selecting a balanced sample is crucial in statistical research to draw meaningful conclusions. Our proposed algorithm, AGENT-B, works in conjunction with existing methods to achieve this balance efficiently. By applying particle swarm optimization to evaluate multiple scenarios simultaneously, AGENT-B excels in identifying optimal sample configurations quickly. In comparison to traditional approaches, our method demonstrates a significant reduction in processing time across various settings. Additionally, AGENT-B adapts easily to accommodate diverse cost structures, making it an adaptable and versatile solution for balanced sampling needs.

Following the success of deep learning in various computer vision tasks, researchers have recently used direct regression methods to simplify camera calibration. These approaches eliminate the need for complex optimization routines by directly estimating the camera's intrinsic parameters from input images. In a camera calibration task, a novel network is proposed that utilizes a regularizing layer to enhance the stability of direct regression. By incorporating this layer, the network can accurately capture the intrinsic parameters of the camera from multiple images. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate the superiority of the proposed approach over classical methods, showcasing robust results in both synthetic and real-world scenarios. Furthermore, the model's ability to be trained end-to-end facilitates its application in real-world scenarios.

In medical imaging, posterior samples are typically obtained from probabilistic models that mirror the distribution of imaging modalities. However, accessing model posterior directly can be challenging. In this work, we propose a method to utilize Conditional Wasserstein GAN to generate posterior samples based on incomplete and noisy images, also extracting samples from the data distribution corresponding to incomplete images. We validated our approach by reconstructing MRI images from incomplete and noisy data and regenerating posterior samples in computed tomography. Results were compared with deep unfolding network and prior-based methods. Code is available at: \url{https://github.com/ghulamalmustafa/CGANWassersteinGAN}

This paper explores the concept of almost invariant subspaces in fractional order systems and establishes corresponding criteria for these subspaces to remain intact. Theoretical findings are supported by numerical examples illustrating almost invariant properties in both discrete and continuous setups.

In this study, we propose a dynamic beam training technique to optimize multi-hop THz links, which learns from feedback and adapts quickly due to its short coherence time. By combining an iterative algorithm with approximate feedback, we improve beam training efficiency by a factor of $R_c/\lambda$, where $R_c$ is the communication bandwidth and $\lambda$ is the carrier frequency, through reduced training sessions. Through numerical simulations, we demonstrate that our proposed method reduces energy consumption and increases data transfer rates in beam training.

We've carried out high-sensitivity radio telescope observations of the well-known binary pulsar, PSR B1133+16, for approximately 420 days. Our analysis of these observations, conducted at the Arecibo Observatory, allowed us to identify multiple scattering screens between the Earth and the pulsar. A total of five individual screens were detected, with three of them observed during a 140-day window. Notably, three of these screens are relatively far from Earth, located at distances of approximately 10 to 20 light years, which makes them significant for further study in the context of the galactic disk.

Deep neural network architectures used in speech analysis have typically consisted of identical transformation layers. Nonetheless, speech exhibits marked periodic patterns, specifically in the duration between consecutive same-syllable utterances. This phenomenon can be captured through a cascaded network layout, where each module is tasked with extracting features from increasingly longer input segments. We introduce a novel cascaded network architecture optimized for periodic signal analysis. In this setup, modules with periodic data extraction capabilities are optimized through a proposed iterative approach. Our results indicate that this method surpasses conventional optimization techniques and achieves superior performance on speech synthesis tasks, ultimately enabling the creation of highly realistic voices.

Human annotators spend significant time and resources manually labeling and preparing text data for the machine learning models that will ultimately rely on it. As data sizes increase, the need for efficient annotation becomes more critical. We believe that achieving this efficiency requires more than simply streamlining the annotation process, but also addressing the fundamental challenges posed by complex tasks and poorly preconditioned data for model training. To tackle these issues, we propose an innovative approach that integrates human and machine learning capabilities within an interactive data augmentation framework. By doing so, we anticipate a 5x reduction in annotation costs for certain tasks. To validate our method's viability, we designed an experiment involving the annotation of 10,000 documents and observed a notable decrease in annotation time per thousand documents (from 278 to 73) and a concurrent improvement in model performance.

The evolving nature of planetary atmospheres remains an unsolved problem in astrophysics and planetary sciences. A key factor in these systems, where temperatures and chemical compositions vary significantly, is the presence of gas-phase species which form through complex non-linear processes. In this study, we use a multi-dimensional atmospheric model to examine how metal-rich atmospheres influence the occurrence of CO, CO2, and NH3 in planets similar to Earth, and how these species interact with UV radiation, chemical reactions, and precipitation processes. By analyzing how these processes change with increasing metal content in models of Earth, super-Earths, and mini-Neptunes, we find that even small enhancements in metallicity can lead to significant increases in gas abundance, particularly in planets with temperatures between 200K and 400K. These temperature ranges also exhibit the greatest variability in gas abundance from 1 to 5 times the solar metallicity. In this range, we identify key processes such as photochemical reactions, gas precipitation, and metal oxide particle interactions as controlling the abundance of CO, CO2, and NH3. Notably, we find that volatile-rich cores can contribute to enhanced CO2 levels. These findings highlight the importance of accurately modeling atmospheric metallicity and core composition in order to make informed predictions about observable properties, such as spectroscopic signatures, that are critical for future comparisons with observational data.

We've developed a new Gutzwiller mean-field theory that can account for both
local interactions and non-Mesoscopic regions in the study of topological insulators.
We use this theory to examine the impact of local coupling and non-Mesoscopic regions
on zero-energy peak formation at finite temperatures, and our findings show that
the peak height exhibits a peak-like structure as the temperature decreases, and this
temperature-dependent behavior is a fundamental property of the system regardless of
the presence of local interactions or non-Mesoscopic regions.

Mobile road inspection applications require efficient methods for navigating roads.
Techniques like Monte Carlo tree search can be used for this purpose, but they may not be
optimal for large-scale areas and can be influenced by their algorithmic parameters.
We present RoadAtlas, a dataset and associated methods for navigating large areas
that can be used to evaluate search algorithms via a modular approach.
Our results show that employing RoadAtlas enhances the efficiency of road inspection
procedures by at least 50% in real-world scenarios.
We also find that non-specialized techniques like value function optimization can
achieve comparable performance to mobile robot search algorithms while withstanding
variations in algorithmic parameters.

Building on the theory of topological Hochschild homology for bicategories, we establish an equivalence between THH(B) and the functor HH(B) for bicategories B, where HH(B) represents the extension of algebraic K-theory to topological algebraic K-theory within the context of shadows. This connection enables us to express THH(B) through the algebraic K-theory of shadows, achieving a geometric interpretation of THH(B). The resulting picture suggests that the integer part of the point-set topological space associated with THH(B) can be seen as the homotopy group of a simplicial set closely related to the shadow of B.

Sound source localization is a complex task that requires identifying the position of a sound-generating object within a scene based on the sounds emitted. The field of sound source localization faces significant challenges due to the diversity of its applications, which include enhancing video descriptions and editing videos automatically. To advance beyond basic methods, a robust evaluation metric and comprehensive dataset are essential. In response to the existing limitations of the FSD50K dataset, which solely provides a classification framework, the VGG-Sound Source (VGG-SS) benchmark offers a more comprehensive set of tasks including classification, localization, and segmentation. By incorporating additional annotation data, the VGG-SS dataset consists of 50,000 classes and offers precise sound source positions, background mask annotations, and audio clips. The VGG-SS dataset stands out with its complex sound sources, extensive class hierarchy, and challenging evaluation protocols, which have shown potential for state-of-the-art performance on semantic segmentation tasks.

This paper introduces a novel framework for graph representation learning in the Lorentzian space. Inspired by recent successes of hyperbolic graph convolutional networks (HGCNs), we develop the Lorentzian graph convolutional network (LGCN), which enhances existing HGCNs by utilizing geometric constraints to optimize node features using gradient descent. Furthermore, LGCN is an inclusive framework subsuming HGCNs, and we provide an innovative approach to optimize LGCN's parameters through a linear transformation. Comprehensive experiments validate the efficacy of our model, demonstrating superior performance in clustering and node classification tasks across various real-world datasets, while also providing intuitive visualizations of node embeddings in the Lorentzian space. All code and datasets are available at https://github.com/yeyong9999/LGCN.

This paper explores recent stability results in inverse problems for partial differential equations, demonstrating how specific inequalities can provide a foundation for observability estimates and ultimately, stability measures. Specifically, we examine the role of observability inequalities derived from Carleman estimates in determining the uniqueness and stability of solutions to inverse problems. We then apply these concepts to a specific model, an inverse problem for the Schr\"{o}dinger equation, to illustrate the implementation of these ideas in a practical context.

In a optomechanical system that combines both classical and quantum components, we observe a unique Total Reflection Symmetry (TSS) effect when changing the cavity length. This TSS effect is linked to the formation of TSS states and can be perceived as a reflection of a incoming light wave. Additionally, our research shows that this optomechanical TSS state can be utilized in a sensor for detecting tiny changes in reflection intensity, effectively providing a solution for invasive intensity-based sensors.

We explore the presence of atoms in u-calculus, an extension of modal u-calculus, both theoretically and practically. In theory, we investigate how the presence of arbitrary rules for atomic formulas affects the computability of satisfiability in u-calculus, building on existing results. We demonstrate that every decision procedure for satisfiability in u-calculus can be expanded to encompass rules for atomic formulas, even those with no clear connection to the existing logic. Furthermore, we present an instance of a logical system for which no decision procedure exists, showcasing that the presence of atoms can significantly impact the complexity of satisfiability in u-calculus. On the practical side, we introduce AtomFinder, an automated tool for determining whether a particular instance of a u-calculus formula's class has members that correspond to real worlds. AtomFinder can also be adapted for application to various types and logics of u-calculus.

The Tsallis distribution has been extensively used in various applications despite being ill-defined mathematically. Recent work has provided an explanation for its occurrence and a method to optimize its parameters. Here, an analogy between the Tsallis distribution and non-equilibrium statistical mechanics has been found, which suggests that the Tsallis distribution represents a steady-state condition in systems with constant energy flow. A new method has been developed to identify the Tsallis distribution's parameters, which can be used to study and simulate complex systems. This method is applied to models of social systems, including a model of preference evolution based on imitation, which provides a quantifiable description of the Tsallis distribution's parameters in relation to the system's dynamics. A second application involves a model of activity choice with a learning mechanism, which yields analytical expressions for the Tsallis distribution's parameters. Both of these results demonstrate that the Tsallis distribution naturally emerges in a broad category of systems that include those with constant energy flow and fractional losses.

We've re-examined the linearized gravity theory known as the de Donder gauge, which includes a mass term for the gravitational perturbations. This mass term was previously found to be inconsistent, as it includes an unwanted degree of freedom. To address this issue, we determined the appropriate coordinate transformation to achieve a healthy, massive linearized gravity theory. By applying a straightforward algebraic technique, we derived the desired coordinate transformation and associated primary fields for this theory. The resulting transformation eliminates the extra degree of freedom, which is now confined to a mass term within the algebraic structure. Additionally, our method enables explicit expression of the primary fields in terms of the physical fields. Consequently, our findings facilitate a deeper understanding of the linearized gravity theory with a mass term, which may have implications for effective theories of gravity.

Given a signed graph, its double cover can be transformed into a regular graph by removing specific edge pairs identified as "frustrations." Conversely, any planar regular graph corresponds to a signed graph double cover, with the potential to identify and remove its frustrations to obtain a planar graph. A new conjecture proposes that for any signed graph, its double cover has a planar equivalent if and only if it contains at most the number of frustrations conjectured by Shahrokh and Foukal in 2019. Through a new generalization, we show that this conjecture holds for a specific class of graphs, and further, that any extended double cover of a planar signed graph with the number of frustrations exceeding a specific higher bound necessarily includes a subgraph whose extended double cover contains a K_{3,3} or a complete bipartite graph of any higher order, or a thunderbolt or a wheel of any higher order, or an extended double cover of a complete triad with a vertex of degree 4. This generalization is applicable to any class of graphs that can be derived from a set of basic graphs, and its proof relies on a new technique involving the restricted application of graph homomorphisms in a reverse order.

We clarify the distinct characteristics of Hamiltonian dynamics within three specific scenarios: quantum equilibrium states, time-independent and time-dependent Hamiltonians, and periodic and non-periodic Hamiltonians. In doing so, we establish a general framework for classifying and distinguishing these dynamics from one another.

The concept of negative temperature is often misunderstood or misrepresented.
A simple two-level system provides an effective framework for demonstrating negative
temperature through clear, numerically measurable parameters. We investigate the
thermodynamic properties of this system after it has reached negative temperature.
We calculate the specific heat and heat capacity for both orthogonal and degenerate
two-level systems, and then analyze these quantities at negative temperatures.
Additionally, we explore the time dependence of these thermodynamic properties
following a quantum jump in the orthogonal case. Our findings may hold relevance
for the study of negative temperature in laser-driven three-level systems.

Let's consider a finite set of integers, denoted as $A$, and an integer $k$; we're interested in understanding the minimum possible value of $x$ such that there exist $x$ integers, collectively representing elements from $A$, which, when summed with appropriate signs, equal $k$. This concept is represented by the function $|x\sigma(A)|$. Initially, we explore how $|x\sigma(A)|$ evolves as $x$ increases, especially focusing on cases where $x$ is substantial, and $A$ has an inherent structure. Furthermore, we aim to identify instances where $|x\sigma(A)|$ grows significantly, even when $x$ is large, and $A$ has a specific pattern. To achieve this, we establish upper limits for $|x\sigma(A)|$, taking into account the distribution of elements within $A$, as well as lower bounds that account for instances where the sum is minimal. Ultimately, we investigate cases where $|x\sigma(A)|$ exceeds a certain high value, and we determine that this situation occurs for various values of $x$ and almost any structure of $A$.

A key factor in preventing colorectal cancer is removing and examining colorectal polyps. Artificial intelligence (AI) has enhanced accuracy in classifying and evaluating the severity of adenomas through deep learning, despite validity concerns due to limited understanding of complex model decisions. To address this, we developed a novel explanation technique, combining saliency analysis and linear regression, to delve into the relationships between apparent skin and underlying colonic tissues, as well as how these relationships affect classification outcomes. Applying this technique to 1350 images from the CRC-AI dataset, we observed a strong correlation between explanations and actual tissue presence/absence. Furthermore, we identified instances (about 4%) where explanations incorrectly indicated the presence of colonic tissue, which were verified and removed from the dataset. Through subsequent re-training, our network's accuracy improved, and validity concerns were addressed.

Research on solving complex acoustic scattering problems has been given significant attention in recent years, particularly those characterized by rapidly varying solutions and high-frequency non-uniformity. To tackle this, researchers have used a combination of asymptotic techniques and approximation methods such as the short-wave asymptotic expansion, high-frequency uniform bounds, and approximate rational decomposition. While these methods have yielded desirable outcomes in the past, they do come with a limitation of relying on human intuition for key parameters. The primary contribution of this work is the development of a fully automated procedure for solving such complex problems. This proposed method leverages a combination of symbolic mathematics and numerical solving capabilities to efficiently handle parametric equations and identify critical points of discontinuity. Through the application of a non-standard technique utilizing symbolic variables, the method also accurately captures the effects of fractional frequency convergence and Wrinkles. The method has been thoroughly tested on five diverse benchmark problems, showcasing its ability to produce highly precise solutions and efficiently converge even in presence of difficult-to-model plate-like geometries.

Water contents within recent Antarctic finds of O chondrites, specifically 2003 Hegyi Hills, 2009 Benenitra, 2013 Chelyabinsk, and their metamorphic equivalents, vary from 0.89 to 1.49 wt% water, demonstrating a notable increase from 0.46 wt% water content typical of ancient O chondrites. Notably, the water levels in Benenitra and Chelyabinsk, ranging from 0.89 to 1.49 wt%, exhibit considerable variation, with an average of approximately 1 wt%. This level of water content is consistent with the amounts needed to create the hydrated silicate minerals observed in these meteorites. In contrast, water levels within the antigorite serpentine metamorphic equivalents of Benenitra and Chelyabinsk, at 0.46 to 0.50 wt%, are significantly lower. These results provide further evidence of the multiple preterrestrial histories of O chondrites, with varying water and oxygen reserves that can lead to different types of lithologies during subsequent planetary processing.

To understand the behavior of our research, consider an infinite chain with interactions, specifically one with spins that follow the XXZ model but with higher spin levels and extra properties. If this chain can be reinterpreted as a part of a larger, integrated system with known properties, determining its behavior can be framed as solving a problem of integration for a known set of equations. A key aspect to analyze in this process is how probabilities or average values change over time, which can be calculated by looking at the interactions between different parts of the system in a mathematical space called the algebra. In our specific case, we show that by using an integrated approach and focusing on a particular type of interaction called the monodromy matrix, we can express these probabilities or average values as a solution to a set of closed equations in the algebra. This allows us to identify specific elements of the algebra that, when combined in a certain way, result in the desired probabilities or average values. This composition of elements is given a specific name and is recognized as belonging to a broader class of known structures, which provides a connection to other areas of mathematics and physics. This understanding helps us to derive additional specific results, which include expressing these probabilities or average values in a way that takes into account the strength of the interactions, given by a parameter called $\gamma$. When this parameter is set to zero, the behavior simplifies to match known results for finite-sized chains. Additionally, our approach allows us to directly calculate certain aspects of the system

This study tackles the challenge of zero-shot speech translation. Our proposed framework, which leverages pre-trained models for speech and text, uses alignment-based speech-to-text and text-to-speech translation, significantly enhances performance in few-shot scenarios (e.g., $10$ sentences). To further improve results, we introduce two techniques: leveraging structural information and a score-based framework for prosodic transfer. The proposed methods yield significant gains of $4.3$ BLEU points in zero-shot settings and $2.4$ BLEU points in zero-shot with domain adaptation, outperforming strong baselines using multi-task learning. Our framework's effectiveness is demonstrated through various evaluations, including human assessments of naturalness and meaning preservation, which shows potential for speech translation in real-world applications.

In this work, we've developed a novel set of multipoles, namely extended dual multipoles, that effectively capture electromagnetic scattering patterns. Building upon previous research, we've demonstrated that these new multipoles surpass conventional ones in accuracy, and that they find application in enhancing the performance of narrowband metasurfaces that combine reflection and transmission properties. A key advantage of our proposed method is its efficiency in computation, as it does not require adjustment of external parameters. A key finding of our analysis is the identification of a compact, annular structure as the fundamental unit for describing electromagnetic scattering, which provides a crucial insight into the design of high-performance narrowband metasurfaces. A key benefit of our approach is its ability to remedy inaccuracy in calculated far-field effects resulting from the use of local approximations. A key outcome of our research is the development of an accelerated boundary wave expansion method tailored for discrete multipoles, enabling the precise calculation of electromagnetic scattering from complex structures composed of array units. This method proves particularly useful in modeling complex metasurfaces characterized by dense unit cells, and provides a valuable tool for reducing the size of computational models while maintaining high accuracy.

Following the Harish-Chandra isomorphism, Mirkovic-Vusovic and Littelmann established a correspondence between weight functions of highest weight modules and shifted Schur polynomials. Building upon this correspondence, we have discovered a similar link between Schur elements and shifted Schur polynomials, with our analysis indicating it may be a part of a broader extension of the Harish-Chandra isomorphism.

We've developed a straightforward, many-electrodes method to tackle the challenge of dark matter stability and the dark parity symmetry in a seesaw framework. In this approach, we've added a minimal dark sector with its own degree of freedom, which is connected to the standard model through several channels. Utilizing a dark parity symmetry, we've divided the new particles into two categories: those with zero impact on dark matter stability and those capable of influencing it. As a result, we've derived a model-independent criterion to ensure dark matter stability. Furthermore, we've established that incorporating a dark Higgs boson is incompatible with the given framework. Additionally, we've identified new, induced neutrino masses as a consequence of the dark sector's presence, which provides a connection between dark matter and experimental neutrino data.

We have developed a semi-phenomenological theory to account for strong spin-orbit coupling in transition metal oxides, incorporating the effects of itinerancy and crystal field splitting. By applying this framework, we have investigated the magnetic properties of 5d electrons in these materials, particularly focusing on the influence of spin-orbit coupling, electron correlation, and crystal field energy on magnetic behavior. Our findings reveal that spin-orbit coupling can be an important interacting phenomenon, rather than a mere additive effect, and should be considered when studying transition metal oxides, especially those with weak to intermediate coupling where the structure of quantum Hall states is shaped by both spin-orbit coupling and correlation effects.

This study introduces relative $I$-functions for toric complete intersections with smooth components, establishing their connection via the $\mathcal{L}$-function in the context of Arita-Minkowski-Hirai's conjecture. Additionally, it demonstrates that the relative $I$-functions share a divisor-theoretic relationship, mirroring the association of Chow groups with algebraic cycles.

This paper will discuss the potential consequences of using sophisticated deep learning models that automatically generate medical image representations, particularly in scenarios where an unseen variation in patient data can significantly alter an image. We will utilize Unsupervised Domain Translation technology to create a scenario where an artist can modify latent code representations of different diseases, including those with limited training data, and explore how this technique affects the consistency of representations across various conditions in the health domain. We will also introduce a novel technique, called Retrospective Labeling, that allows for accurate annotations of medical image categories without initial labels. Our method involves first translating representations of undiagnosed conditions into known disease categories, then identifying the nearest neighbor in a pre-trained dataset of healthy individuals to determine the actual diagnosis. We have conducted extensive experiments on two public datasets of retinal images, along with one internal dataset of breast cancer images, to evaluate the effectiveness of our method. Results show that our technique can achieve high accuracy rates when comparing undiagnosed conditions to known categories, but requires additional supervision to achieve high precision rates.

ViDaExpert is an intuitive data exploration tool designed for multimedia retrieval datasets, allowing users to interactively visualize three-dimensional data spaces and assess dimensionality reduction representations. Despite being tailored for these specific datasets, ViDaExpert offers a comprehensive solution for various data visualization needs. Its key features encompass: dynamic 3D data visualization, enabled by JavaScript and Three.js; an user-friendly interface, facilitating easy interaction with three-dimensional environments; and a comprehensive set of techniques for dimensionality reduction, including Multimedia Retrieval Rank preservation (MRRP). By providing an intuitive visualization of three-dimensional data spaces, incorporating actual data points, ViDaExpert can be employed to evaluate the performance of dimensionality reduction methods, pinpoint clusters, and identify outliers. Additionally, ViDaExpert offers an interactive interface for comparing dimensionality reduction techniques, enabled by user-friendly controls and adjustable parameters, allowing users to explore three-dimensional data spaces with ease.

This research develops a higher-order 2D monomial approximation method for approximating functions and their derivatives on unstructured mesh elements. By comparing first-order and second-order methods, we demonstrate how increasing the approximation order significantly improves approximation accuracy, especially when modeling non-smooth functions. However, this benefit comes at a cost of increased computational time and memory usage for higher-order approximations. As an alternative to traditional finite element methods, our monomial-based approach offers greater flexibility and accuracy. To further enhance performance, we propose a strategy for adaptive order adjustment. Numerical examples validate the effectiveness of our methods, including approximate solutions and associated plots.
